title: Gallagher's Third-Quarter Revenue Rises 18% to $3.93 Billion and Adjusted EPS Climbs to $3.00, With Organic Brokerage Growth of 5%
summary: Arthur J. Gallagher & Co. reported third-quarter 2026 revenues of $3,930 million, up from $3,325 million, with net earnings of $406 million, adjusted EPS of $3.00 versus $2.31 and organic brokerage growth of 5%, while acquisition activity fell sharply from a year earlier.
description:
Arthur J. Gallagher & Co., the Illinois-based insurance broker and risk manager, has published its results for the third quarter of 2026. All figures below come from the company's own earnings release for the quarter. The release describes non-GAAP (adjusted) measures that the company defines itself, so the adjusted numbers should be read as management's presentation and not as audited accounting results. This article uses only figures stated in the release, and where it does simple arithmetic of its own, it says so.

The headline numbers

Total revenues before reimbursements were $3,930 million, compared with $3,325 million in the third quarter of 2025. The brokerage segment contributed $3,473 million, against $2,922 million a year earlier, and the risk management segment, which handles claims administration and loss control for clients that self-insure, contributed $457 million, against $402 million. A simple division of those rounded figures gives total revenue growth of about 18%, brokerage growth of about 19% and risk management growth of about 14%. That is arithmetic performed for this article, not a figure quoted from the release, although the chief executive's own summary also refers to revenue growth of 18%.

Net earnings were $406 million, or $1.55 per diluted share, up from $273 million, or $1.04 per share. The company also reports adjusted net earnings, which remove items such as acquisition-related costs and amortization. On that basis, adjusted net earnings were $782 million, or $3.00 per diluted share, compared with $604 million, or $2.31 per share. Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, amortization and change in estimated acquisition earnout payables, known as EBITDAC, were $1,048 million, against $812 million. Adjusted EBITDAC was $1,253 million, against $1,013 million. Within that, adjusted EBITDAC for brokerage was $1,222 million, against $975 million, and for risk management was $104 million, against $89 million.

Organic growth

Organic growth strips out the effect of acquisitions, disposals and currency, and it is the measure analysts watch most closely for a broker because it shows how much of the growth comes from selling more to existing clients. Gallagher reported brokerage organic growth of 5% for the quarter, with base commissions and fees growing 4%. The risk management segment reported organic fee growth of 10%. The release does not give a forecast for organic growth, and it contains no formal guidance for 2026. A 4% to 5% organic rate is lower than the double-digit organic growth that large brokers reported in the hard market of recent years, which is consistent with the cooling of property and casualty pricing that other insurers' results this season have described. The release itself does not draw that link, so it is offered here as context, not as the company's explanation.

Margins

The adjusted brokerage EBITDAC margin was 35.3%, up from 33.3% a year earlier, and the adjusted risk management margin was 22.8%, up from 21.9%. Margins matter because a broker's costs, mainly people, are largely fixed in the short run, so revenue growth that outpaces cost growth widens the margin. The release reports the improvement but does not break down how much came from cost control and how much from revenue mix.

Nine-month figures

For the first nine months of 2026, revenues were $12,601 million, against $10,192 million, which is about 24% higher by simple division. Net earnings were $1,553 million, or $5.97 per diluted share, against $1,350 million, or $5.16 per share. Adjusted earnings per share were $10.32, against $8.35. Adjusted EBITDAC was $4,204 million, against $3,454 million. The nine-month adjusted brokerage margin was 36.5%, below the 37.9% of the same period a year earlier, while the risk management adjusted margin rose to 22.4% from 21.1%. The nine-month brokerage margin is therefore lower than a year ago even though the third-quarter margin improved, a reminder that the quarterly and year-to-date pictures are not identical.

Acquisitions have slowed

Gallagher built much of its recent growth through acquisitions. In the third quarter of 2026 it completed five brokerage mergers with about $102 million of estimated annualized revenue. In the third quarter of 2025 it completed six, with about $3,036 million of annualized revenue, a figure dominated by one very large deal, the AssuredPartners acquisition. Over nine months, it completed 19 brokerage acquisitions with about $209 million of annualized revenue, against 25 with about $3,390 million. The release also notes that the third quarter of 2025 brokerage results included about $76 million of interest income related to the financing of the AssuredPartners deal, which affects year-over-year comparisons. Revenue growth of 18% therefore reflects, in part, a full quarter of acquired businesses that were not owned for the whole of the prior-year period, and not only underlying demand.

What management said

The chief executive, J. Patrick Gallagher Jr., said in the release that the company delivered another excellent quarter. He pointed to the 26th consecutive quarter of double-digit growth in adjusted EBITDAC, with revenue up 18% and adjusted EBITDAC up 25%. A division of the rounded adjusted EBITDAC figures in the release ($1,253 million over $1,013 million) gives about 24%, so the 25% he cites may reflect unrounded amounts or a different basis; readers wanting the exact figure should check the company's reconciliation tables. These are the company's own characterizations.

What to watch

Three questions follow from the release. First, whether organic growth holds at 4% to 5% as commercial property pricing continues to soften, since lower premiums reduce the commission base even when clients buy more cover. Second, whether acquisition activity returns to a larger scale or stays at the smaller pace shown this year. Third, whether the margin gains seen in the third quarter can persist when the nine-month brokerage margin is still below the prior year.

Limits

This article summarizes a company earnings release and does not include independent analysis, analyst estimates or share-price reaction. Adjusted figures are non-GAAP measures defined by the company. It is general information, not investment advice.
source_name: Arthur J. Gallagher & Co. (third-quarter 2026 earnings release)
image_alt: Financial documents and calculator representing quarterly earnings (illustrative)
key_points: Total revenues before reimbursements were $3,930 million, up from $3,325 million a year earlier; brokerage revenue was $3,473 million and risk management revenue was $457 million.
Net earnings were $406 million ($1.55 diluted EPS) versus $273 million ($1.04); adjusted net earnings were $782 million, or $3.00 per share, versus $604 million, or $2.31.
Brokerage organic growth was 5%, with base commissions and fees up 4%, and risk management organic fee growth was 10%.
Adjusted EBITDAC rose to $1,253 million from $1,013 million, and the adjusted brokerage margin widened to 35.3% from 33.3%.
Gallagher closed five brokerage acquisitions with about $102 million of annualized revenue in the quarter, against six deals with about $3,036 million a year earlier.
why_it_matters: Gallagher is one of the world's largest insurance brokers, so its results show how commercial insurance buyers and sellers are behaving. Slower organic growth than in recent years, a much smaller acquisition pipeline than last year and higher margins give a clear read on how brokers are earning money as insurance prices cool.

title: Australia's Cyclone Reinsurance Pool Passes A$1 Billion in Claims Paid After Its Busiest Season, but Strata Mitigation Discounts Total Just A$1,716
summary: The Australian Reinsurance Pool Corporation's 2025-26 annual report says the cyclone pool has paid more than A$1 billion in claims since 2022 after nine declared cyclone events, without drawing on its A$10 billion government guarantee, while premium discounts for mitigation had reached only A$1,716 for strata buildings.
description:
The Australian Reinsurance Pool Corporation, known as ARPC, has published its annual report for 2025-26, and Insurance Business Australia reported its main findings on October 29, 2026. ARPC is a government-owned body that runs two schemes: a cyclone reinsurance pool, which backs insurers selling cover in cyclone-prone northern Australia, and a terrorism reinsurance pool. The details below come from that trade-press report; the annual report itself was not reviewed. Where this article does arithmetic of its own, it says so.

A busy season and more than A$1 billion paid

The cyclone pool began operating in 2022. According to the report, it has now paid more than A$1 billion in claims since it started, and 2025-26 was its busiest season to date, with nine declared cyclone events. A reinsurance pool works behind the scenes. Homeowners, strata bodies and businesses buy insurance from their usual insurer, and the insurer in turn buys reinsurance from the pool for cyclone losses, so the pool pays the insurer, not the policyholder directly. ARPC's chief executive, Dr Christopher Wallace, is quoted as saying that despite a high level of cyclone activity, ARPC met all claims and financial obligations.

The financial position

ARPC reported gross written premiums of A$1.092 billion for the year and net assets of about A$1.818 billion at June 30, 2026. The report says ARPC met all of its obligations without drawing on the A$10 billion Commonwealth guarantee that stands behind the cyclone pool. That guarantee is the backstop if claims exceed the pool's own resources, and the fact that it has not been used is the main sign that the pool's funding held up through the season. The report does not give the number of individual claims paid, the size of the largest event or the pool's reinsurance programme, so the scale of the season can be judged only from the headline figures.

Who is covered

The pool's exposure is large. The report says 72,500 strata buildings and 101,000 small business buildings in northern Australia are covered, along with about 3 million homes. Strata buildings are apartment blocks and townhouse complexes in which owners share a single insurance policy, so a single building can contain many households. The average annual cyclone pool premium is A$801 for each strata risk and A$240 for each small business risk. Those are the pool's own premiums, which are only one component of what policyholders pay. The report does not give an average for homes.

Mitigation discounts: a small number

The more striking finding concerns mitigation. A mitigation discount is a reduction in premium given to an owner who strengthens a building against cyclone damage, for example by upgrading roofs, tie-downs or windows. The idea is that cheaper cover rewards investment in resilience, which reduces future losses. The report gives the figures at June 30, 2026:

Residential: A$9.39 million in annual premium reductions.

Strata: A$1,716 in total since the strata discount began applying on April 1, 2025.

Small and medium businesses: nothing so far. The business discount became effective on April 1, 2026, and was developed with the Cyclone Testing Station at James Cook University.

The strata total is small in two senses. It is a tiny sum next to a pool that collects more than A$1 billion in premiums a year, and it is tiny next to a covered population of 72,500 strata buildings. Simple arithmetic on those two figures, done for this article and not reported, (A$1,716 divided by 72,500 buildings) works out to about two cents per building across the covered population, a spread that suggests very few buildings have qualified. The report does not explain why uptake is low. Possible reasons include the cost of upgrades, the time needed to assess a building, and the recent start of the strata scheme, but those are speculation here and the report does not attribute the low figure to any of them. ARPC says a review of premium rates for 2026 is underway.

The terrorism pool

The terrorism pool has a very different profile. The report says there were no claims arising from the Bondi Beach incident on December 14, 2025, because the losses were within insurers' own retentions, meaning the amount an insurer bears before the pool responds. It also says there were no losses from the Perth CBD incident on January 26, 2026. The pool therefore paid nothing for either event. The report does not describe either incident in detail, and this article does not either.

Why the numbers matter

For policyholders in northern Australia, the pool exists because cyclone cover had become very expensive or hard to obtain. The report's main message about payments is reassuring: a busy season did not exhaust the pool. The mitigation numbers, by contrast, suggest that the link between spending on resilience and paying less for insurance is not yet working for most owners. If the discount remains tiny, owners have less financial reason to strengthen buildings, and the policy goal of reducing future losses is harder to meet. The premium review ARPC mentions is the next point at which the discount design could change.

What is not in the report

The trade-press report does not give the number of claims, the ombudsman's role, the pool's reinsurance cost or the planned changes from the premium review. Readers who need those details should consult ARPC's annual report directly.

Limits

This article relies on a single trade-press summary of the annual report and does not reproduce it. Figures are as reported. It is general information, not insurance or financial advice.
source_name: Insurance Business Australia, reporting the ARPC 2025-26 annual report (October 29, 2026)
image_alt: Storm clouds over a coastline representing cyclone risk (illustrative)
key_points: The Cyclone Reinsurance Pool has paid more than A$1 billion in claims since it began operating in 2022, and 2025-26 was its busiest season, with nine declared cyclone events.

ARPC reported gross written premiums of A$1.092 billion and net assets of about A$1.818 billion at June 30, 2026, and says it met all obligations without drawing on the A$10 billion Commonwealth guarantee.
Mitigation discounts at June 30, 2026 amounted to A$9.39 million of annual premium reductions for residential buildings, A$1,716 in total for strata buildings, and nothing yet for small businesses.

The pool covers about 72,500 strata buildings, 101,000 small business buildings and roughly 3 million homes in northern Australia, with average annual cyclone pool premiums of A$801 per strata risk and A$240 per small business risk.

The terrorism pool recorded no claims for the Bondi Beach incident of December 14, 2025, where losses sat within insurers' retentions, or for the Perth CBD incident of January 26, 2026, where there were no losses.
why_it_matters: Australia created a government-backed reinsurance pool so that home, strata and business owners in cyclone country could buy affordable cover. The annual report shows the pool paying real claims at scale, and it also shows how little reward policyholders have so far received for strengthening their buildings.

title: FCA's Multifirm Review of Frontier AI and Cyber Resilience Sets Out Five Themes and No New Rules: Vulnerabilities Are Being Found Faster Than Firms Can Fix Them
summary: The UK Financial Conduct Authority's multifirm review of frontier AI and cyber resilience, summarised by law firms in September and October 2026, reports five themes drawn from what firms said, led by the finding that vulnerability discovery is outpacing firms' ability to respond, and states that it creates no new rules or expectations.
description:
The UK Financial Conduct Authority has published the findings of a multifirm review on how frontier artificial intelligence is affecting cyber resilience in financial services. This article is based on law-firm summaries of the review, principally A&O Shearman's finreg note, which dates the FCA publication to September 2026, and a UK insurance newsletter from the firm Sidley dated October 30, 2026. The FCA's own page could not be reviewed, so the descriptions below are those of the summaries, and the exact wording of the FCA may differ. The summaries do not say how many firms took part or give quantitative data, and this article does not supply any.

What kind of document it is

The first point the summaries make is about status. The review does not create new rules, and the FCA does not set new expectations in it. It reports observations that participating firms shared with the regulator. That distinction matters for compliance teams: a document that says it creates no new expectations still shows what supervisors are paying attention to, and firms that cannot answer the questions it raises should expect to be asked them. According to the Sidley newsletter, the review follows a joint statement made in May by the FCA, the Bank of England and HM Treasury on the same subject. The summaries describe frontier AI in general terms as the most capable current AI systems, including those that can analyse code and find software flaws; they do not name particular models or companies.

The five themes

As summarised, the review organises its findings into five themes.

1. Vulnerability discovery is outpacing firms' ability to respond. A vulnerability is a flaw in software or configuration that an attacker could exploit. If AI tools make flaws easier and faster to find, the number of flaws to be addressed rises faster than the capacity to fix them. The review's point is that finding problems is no longer the main bottleneck; remediation is.

2. Frontier AI is a test of organisational resilience, not only a tool. The summary says firms should think of it as something that stresses the whole organisation, including how decisions are made under pressure, and not merely as a product that security teams adopt.

3. The value firms get depends on the operating environment around the AI, which the review calls the harness. That includes governance, tooling, controls and human oversight. In other words, the same AI system will deliver different results in a firm with clean asset inventories and clear ownership than in one without.

4. Frontier AI exposes existing weaknesses. The summaries list four: vulnerability management, access management, dependency mapping and remediation. Dependency mapping means knowing which systems and suppliers rely on which others, so that a flaw in one component can be traced to the services it affects. A firm that lacks that map cannot easily judge how urgent a given flaw is.

5. Governance and human judgement remain critical. Even where AI speeds up analysis, people must decide priorities, accept risk and take responsibility for outcomes.

The questions the FCA puts to firms

The summaries describe three groups of questions. The first concerns ownership and guardrails: who in the firm is accountable for the use of frontier AI in security work, and what limits apply. The second concerns whether vulnerability management and change management remain effective when the volume and speed of findings rise. Change management is the process by which software updates are tested and released, and faster fixes put pressure on it, since a rushed patch can itself cause an outage. The third concerns whether the firm can operate under pressure, meaning whether its incident response and decision-making hold up when many problems arrive at once.

What this means for insurers and brokers

The review is addressed to FCA-regulated firms generally, and the summaries do not single out insurers. For insurers and intermediaries, the practical consequences are those that follow from the themes. A firm's patching speed, its supplier mapping and its access controls are the matters the review asks about, and they also bear on the cyber risk that insurers underwrite for their customers. The summaries do not say that the FCA expects any change to cyber insurance, and this article does not suggest it.

A worked illustration

Consider a hypothetical firm whose tools report 200 new flaws in a month, up from 50, while its team can fix 60 a month. Before the change the backlog shrank; afterwards it grows by 140 a month. This is an invented example for illustration, not data from the review, but it captures the first theme: when discovery speeds up and remediation capacity stays the same, the queue lengthens, and the firm must either raise capacity or get better at deciding which flaws matter most.

What is not known

The summaries leave several questions unanswered. They do not say how many firms participated, which sectors were included or whether any firm was criticised. They do not quantify how much faster vulnerability discovery has become. And they do not say whether the FCA plans follow-up work or supervisory action. Readers who need the exact text should consult the FCA's publication.

Limits

This article relies on secondary law-firm summaries and not on the FCA's own document. It is general information, not legal or compliance advice.
source_name: A&O Shearman, summarising the FCA's multifirm review (published September 2026)
image_alt: Code on a computer screen representing cyber security (illustrative)
key_points: The FCA's multifirm review on frontier AI and cyber resilience summarises what firms told the regulator and, according to the law-firm summary, introduces no new rules or expectations.
The first of five themes is that vulnerability discovery is outpacing firms' ability to respond to what is found.

The review treats frontier AI as a test of organisational resilience and not only as a tool, and says the value firms get depends on the surrounding 'harness' of governance, tooling, controls and human oversight.
It says the technology exposes weaknesses in vulnerability management, access management, dependency mapping and remediation, and that governance and human judgement remain critical.
The FCA's questions for firms centre on clear ownership and guardrails, effective vulnerability and change management at higher volume and speed, and the ability to operate under pressure.
why_it_matters: Banks, insurers and brokers regulated by the FCA depend on software that is full of undiscovered flaws. If AI tools let attackers and defenders find those flaws much faster, the limiting factor becomes how quickly a firm can fix them, and the FCA is telling firms where it expects them to look first.

title: New India Assurance Posts a Second-Quarter Loss of Rs 1,267 Crore as Flood Claims, Large Property Losses and a Rs 715 Crore Motor Provision Outweigh a Rs 1,800 Crore NSE Gain
summary: New India Assurance reported a standalone loss after tax of Rs 1,26,704 lakh (about Rs 1,267 crore) for the second quarter of FY27, citing large property and flood claims, a Rs 715 crore motor third-party provision after a Supreme Court ruling and falling property rates, partly offset by about Rs 1,800 crore of gains from selling part of its NSE stake.
description:
New India Assurance Company, one of India's largest general insurers, has reported a loss for the second quarter of the 2026-27 financial year, known in India as Q2 FY27. The figures in this article come from a single secondary report, published by InvestyWise, of the company's standalone results. The company's own filing was not reviewed, and the report does not give prior-year comparisons for most figures, so this article does not make year-on-year claims it cannot support. In this article, 1 lakh is 100,000 and 1 crore is 10 million, and the crore figures are conversions of the lakh amounts reported.

The headline result

The company reported a standalone loss after tax of Rs 1,26,704 lakh for the quarter, which is about Rs 1,267 crore. For the first half of FY27 the loss after tax was Rs 1,52,381 lakh, about Rs 1,524 crore. A simple subtraction, done for this article and not reported, shows that the loss for the first quarter of the year was therefore around Rs 257 crore, so most of the half-year loss arose in the second quarter. Total income was Rs 12,53,939 lakh, about Rs 12,539 crore, for the quarter and Rs 23,77,534 lakh, about Rs 23,775 crore, for the half year.

The operating loss, which measures the result of insurance operations before some other items, was Rs 2,33,014 lakh, about Rs 2,330 crore, for the quarter and Rs 3,13,281 lakh, about Rs 3,133 crore, for the half year. The loss after tax is smaller than the operating loss. The report does not itemise the bridge between the two, but it does mention a large investment gain, described below.

Premium growth

Gross written premium, the total premium booked before reinsurance, grew 5.14% in the quarter. The report's headline calls this gross direct premium, but its body text uses gross written premium, and it does not give the base amounts. Net premium written, the premium retained after reinsurance, was Rs 8,85,042 lakh, about Rs 8,850 crore, for the quarter and Rs 20,07,969 lakh, about Rs 20,080 crore, for the half year. The company said a steep decline in property rates was the main factor affecting premium growth. Property rates are the prices charged for insuring buildings and industrial assets; when they fall, an insurer can grow its book of policies and still collect little more in premium.

Where the losses came from

The report lists several causes. The property segment recorded underwriting losses from multiple large risk losses and from flood claims in Gujarat, North India and the North East of the country. Aviation, motor and health each reported adverse experience in the quarter, which means claims were worse than the insurer expected. In motor insurance the company also made an additional provision of Rs 715 crore for third-party claims. The report ties this to a Supreme Court verdict on compensation for unpaid domestic work, and says there has been no premium revision in that segment. A provision is money set aside for expected future claims, so a provision is recognised as a cost now even though the payments will come later. The report does not explain the legal detail of the ruling or how many claims it affects, and this article does not either.

The investment gain

The one item that worked in the other direction was the partial monetisation of the company's stake in the National Stock Exchange of India. The report says it produced about Rs 1,800 crore in capital gains and calls it the only investment income figure it gives. Comparing the two numbers, done for this article, the gain is more than twice the Rs 715 crore motor provision, which shows how much of the result depended on a sale of a holding and not on insurance operations. A gain from selling a stake is not a recurring source of income, so it cannot be assumed to repeat in later quarters.

Solvency

The solvency ratio was 1.61 times. In India, insurers must hold capital of at least 1.5 times the regulatory minimum, which the report calls the IRDAI control level, so New India Assurance remains above it. The margin is 0.11 turns of cover, which is a calculation made here. The report does not give the solvency ratio for the previous quarter or year, so readers cannot tell from it whether solvency improved or deteriorated.

What is missing from the report

Several useful numbers are absent from the source: the combined ratio, which compares claims and expenses with premium; the claims incurred; the total investment income; and the prior-year comparison. Those would show whether the quarter was worse than usual or typical of a pattern. The source also does not say how much of the property loss was flood-related and how much came from large individual risks.

Why it matters beyond one company

India's general insurance market has seen softer property pricing, as the report notes, while claims from floods and large risks continue to arrive. An insurer that is also the largest in the market feels both effects. The motor third-party provision is a reminder that court rulings on compensation can change the cost of claims for the whole industry, not only for one company, although the report discusses only New India Assurance.

Limits

This article is based on one secondary report of unaudited quarterly results and does not include analyst views or the company's management commentary. Currency conversions are rounded. It is general information, not investment advice.
source_name: InvestyWise, reporting New India Assurance's Q2 FY27 results
image_alt: Financial charts and figures representing quarterly insurer results (illustrative)
key_points: New India Assurance reported a standalone second-quarter FY27 loss after tax of Rs 1,26,704 lakh (about Rs 1,267 crore), taking the first-half loss to Rs 1,52,381 lakh (about Rs 1,524 crore).
Gross written premium grew 5.14%; net premium written was about Rs 8,850 crore for the quarter and about Rs 20,080 crore for the half year, and total income was about Rs 12,539 crore for the quarter.

The operating loss was about Rs 2,330 crore for the quarter, driven by multiple large property risk losses and flood claims in Gujarat, North India and the North East, with adverse experience in aviation, motor and health.

The insurer made an additional provision of Rs 715 crore for motor third-party claims after a Supreme Court verdict on compensation for unpaid domestic work, and booked about Rs 1,800 crore of capital gains from partly selling its NSE stake.
Its solvency ratio was 1.61 times, above the regulator's 1.5 times control level, and the company said falling property rates were the main drag on premium growth.
why_it_matters: New India Assurance is one of India's largest general insurers, so a large quarterly loss is closely watched. The results show how floods, large property claims and a court ruling on motor compensation can overwhelm underwriting, and how one-off investment gains can cushion the result.

title: British Columbia's Restricted Insurance Agency Licence Starts January 1, 2027: Car Dealers and Other Incidental Sellers Face a C$1,000 Application Fee, a Designated Representative and a March 31 Deadline
summary: From January 1, 2027, British Columbia businesses that sell insurance incidentally, including all motor vehicle dealers, need a Restricted Insurance Agency licence from the Insurance Council of BC, with a C$1,000 application fee, a trained designated representative, accredited training for sellers and a March 31, 2027 application deadline for those using earlier exemptions.
description:
British Columbia is introducing a new category of insurance licence for businesses that sell insurance as a side activity. The Restricted Insurance Agent Licence Regulation comes into force on January 1, 2027, and the Insurance Council of BC, the province's insurance regulator for licensing, will issue and oversee the licence. The details below come from the Council's own question-and-answer page about the Restricted Insurance Agency, or RIA, licence. That page says some details, including the full list of eligible business types and insurance products, are set out in the regulation or on pages not reproduced in it, and the application process itself was described as not yet available. This article therefore reports only what the page states.

What the licence is for

The RIA licence lets trained representatives sell insurance under the agency's licence. It is aimed at non-insurance businesses that sell insurance incidental to their ordinary operations. A car dealership that offers insurance related to a vehicle purchase is the clearest example, and the Council states that all motor vehicle dealers qualify, including powersport dealerships. To be eligible, a business must fall within one of the business types listed in the regulation, and the insurance it sells must be among the designated products the regulation lists. Businesses whose primary or only activity is insurance are not eligible, and neither are businesses that want to sell insurance types the regulation does not include. They would need a different licence.

Dates that matter

January 1, 2027: the regulation takes effect.

March 31, 2027: businesses that have been selling insurance incidentally under earlier exemptions must apply for an RIA licence by this date if they want to keep selling insurance.

December 31, 2027: the restricted travel insurance agency licence is discontinued after this date, and former holders cannot conduct insurance business after it. Holders of that licence must transition to the RIA licence. Holders of other product-limited licences can keep and renew them but cannot make changes, and the Council encourages eligible holders to move to the RIA licence.

The designated representative

Every RIA must appoint a designated representative, who must be an officer, director, partner or sole proprietor of the business. The designated representative acts for the business, oversees its insurance activities and is responsible for making sure it complies with the rules. The regulation does not say where the representative must be located, but the person must ensure proper supervision and adherence to the licence conditions.

Before a person can be appointed, they must complete a mandatory designated representative course. A business needs at least one representative who has completed it before applying. The Council describes it as about four hours long, self-paced and possible to complete over several sessions. Access lasts 60 days from registration; if the course is not finished in that time, access expires and the fee must be paid again. The course fee is C$320, which is separate from the application fee, non-refundable and non-transferable. A completion certificate can be downloaded, but it does not have to be submitted because the Council verifies completion itself.

Fees and insurance

The application fee is C$1,000. The annual fee depends on the number of representatives operating under the licence, but the page does not give the amounts and points to another Council page. Errors and omissions insurance is required for insurance activities. That is professional liability cover that pays if a seller's mistake harms a customer. The Council notes that some businesses may already have such cover and suggests consulting their insurer, with detailed requirements set out on its errors and omissions page. As a simple illustration, done for this article, a business that applies with one new designated representative would pay at least C$1,320 in the two fees the page states (C$1,000 plus C$320) before any annual fee, insurance premium or training costs.

Training for people who sell

Employees and non-employee agents who sell insurance must take accredited training for the products they sell. Any insurance training provider can apply for accreditation, and applications opened on October 26, 2026. A provider must submit course materials, an application form and a checklist, and courses must meet performance requirements covering knowledge, technical abilities and business skills. Accreditation lasts four years, after which providers must reapply. Accredited courses will be listed on the Council's website as they become available. Because accredited courses may not exist by January 1, 2027, the Council says it may initially issue a term RIA licence to applicants whose representatives completed non-approved training that still meets the performance requirements, provided all other qualifications are met.

What businesses should do now

The Council's suggested next steps are to review the program information, assess whether the business can meet the qualification and ongoing requirements, prepare business information and the qualification steps, and apply when the licence becomes available. Questions go to ria-licence@insurancecouncilofbc.com.

What the page does not say

The page does not set out enforcement or discipline for RIA licensees. It states only that the designated representative must ensure compliance and that the business must operate within the licence conditions. It does not list the eligible business types or products, and it does not give the annual fee schedule. Businesses should read the regulation and the Council's other pages before relying on this summary.

Limits

This article summarizes a regulator's Q&A page and is not legal advice. Rules and fees may change, and affected businesses should confirm current requirements with the Insurance Council of BC.

image_alt: Cars on a dealership road representing vehicle-related insurance sales (illustrative)
key_points: The Restricted Insurance Agent Licence Regulation takes effect on January 1, 2027, and the Insurance Council of BC will issue and oversee the new Restricted Insurance Agency (RIA) licence for non-insurance businesses that sell insurance incidentally.
All motor vehicle dealers, including powersport dealerships, qualify; businesses whose primary or only activity is insurance do not.
Businesses selling insurance under earlier exemptions must apply by March 31, 2027, and the restricted travel insurance agency licence is discontinued after December 31, 2027.
The application fee is C$1,000, and each business must appoint a designated representative who has completed a roughly four-hour course costing C$320; errors and omissions insurance is also required.
Employees and non-employee agents who sell insurance must take accredited training for the products they sell, and applications from training providers for accreditation opened on October 26, 2026.
why_it_matters: Car dealers, travel agents and other businesses often sell insurance as an add-on to something else. British Columbia is replacing patchwork exemptions with one licence, so customers should get a trained seller and a named person accountable, and businesses face new costs and a deadline.

title: ASIC Sues First Guardian's Former Fund Chiefs Over A$600 Million of Mostly Super Money, Alleging A$57 Million Went to Entities They Controlled, as the Collapse Swells the Compensation Scheme Levy
summary: ASIC has filed civil penalty proceedings in the Federal Court against David Anderson and Simon Selimaj of Falcon Capital over the First Guardian fund, alleging that more than 6,000 investors put in over A$600 million, mostly from superannuation, while the collapse pushes the Compensation Scheme of Last Resort's FY2027 estimate to A$198.1 million; none of the allegations has been proven.
description:
The Australian Securities and Investments Commission, ASIC, has begun civil penalty proceedings in the Federal Court against two former leaders of the company that ran the collapsed First Guardian fund. Insurance Business Australia reported the case on October 30, 2026, and the details below come from that report. The court has made no findings. Every statement about the defendants' conduct in this article is an allegation by ASIC, set out in its claim, and the defendants are presumed to be able to contest it.

Who is being sued

ASIC is suing David Anderson, who was managing director and chief executive of Falcon Capital, the responsible entity of the First Guardian fund, and Simon Selimaj, who was Falcon's executive chairman and chief investment officer. A responsible entity is the company that operates a managed investment scheme and owes duties to the people who invest in it. ASIC is also seeking the court's permission to sue Falcon itself, which is in liquidation. ASIC asks for declarations, penalties and disqualification orders. It says it will not try to collect any penalty from Falcon, so that any remaining funds can go to investors.

What ASIC alleges

According to the report, ASIC alleges that between August 2019 and April 2025, more than 6,000 Australians invested over A$600 million in First Guardian, mostly from their superannuation. It alleges that about A$270 million went into unregistered underlying funds that Falcon controlled, and that at least A$57 million went to entities controlled by Anderson or Selimaj. It also alleges that specific investments were made without proper due diligence or security. The examples reported include investments in the Rogue Traders Group restaurants; Fox Friday Brewing, even though investors were allegedly told the fund would not back alcohol businesses; at least A$15 million to Maleo Indonesia between mid-2020 and mid-2022, with no documents; Maleo Singapore agreements that allegedly put A$188 million of assets on the books that were worth little or nothing; and at least A$27.9 million into property developments.

ASIC further alleges that the product disclosure statements misleadingly described the investment processes as robust, that Anderson made decisions without meaningful oversight and with undisclosed conflicts, and that Selimaj failed to supervise. ASIC chair Sarah Court is quoted as saying: "These were Australians' retirement savings." Anderson's lawyer, Dan Mackay of Mackay Chapman, is reported as saying that the claim runs to more than 150 pages, that his client was served only that day and that ASIC must still prove its case. The report says no public response from Selimaj had been reported.

How much has been recovered

The liquidators, Ross Blakeley and Paul Harlond of FTI Consulting, have reported on recoveries. The directors valued First Guardian's investments at about A$512.8 million. The liquidators have recovered A$8.02 million, which is 1.56%. The recoveries come from three groups. Investments with a book value of about A$117.6 million were written off or settled and returned A$3.49 million. Investments valued at A$50.75 million returned A$4.53 million, and full recovery is not expected. Investments worth about A$344.5 million, mostly offshore property and early-stage technology, have returned nothing. Adding the three groups of book values gives about A$512.9 million, and adding the two sums returned gives A$8.02 million, so the report's figures are consistent with one another (arithmetic done for this article). Legal fees of A$3.33 million and liquidators' fees of A$3.23 million have consumed a large share of recoveries; together they are about A$6.56 million, a sum close to the A$8.02 million recovered, though the report does not say how the fees were funded. Public examinations are due in the coming weeks, and Shield director Paul Chiodo is among those to be examined.

The compensation scheme bill

The Compensation Scheme of Last Resort, or CSLR, pays compensation to consumers when a financial firm that has been found liable by the Australian Financial Complaints Authority cannot pay. In July, the CSLR raised its estimate for FY2027 to A$198.1 million, which includes a A$30.2 million allowance for Shield and First Guardian claims. Of that estimate, A$190.3 million relates to personal financial advice, almost ten times the A$20 million cap for that subsector. About A$170.3 million above the cap must come from a special levy. Treasury's draft special levy plan would charge managed investment scheme responsible entities A$40 million, which would include Falcon, and would raise the share paid by mortgage and finance brokers from about A$668,000 to A$7.79 million. The CSLR has paid out more than A$200 million to more than 1,600 people since April 2024. General insurance brokers are currently outside the scheme, and their industry body, NIBA, has resisted bringing them in.

The insurance questions

The report says the public record does not show whether Falcon or its directors carried directors and officers (D&O) liability insurance or professional indemnity (PI) insurance, or whether any insurer is paying for their defence. It explains how such cover generally works. D&O policies usually pay defence costs, but they typically contain conduct exclusions that apply once dishonesty is proven, and civil penalties are generally treated as uninsurable. The Insurance Council of Australia has told Treasury that PI policies do not cover fraud, criminal conduct or systemic failure, and that moving more of the CSLR cost onto PI would not close the funding gap. The report suggests brokers placing cover for financial institutions should expect tougher renewal discussions about platform onboarding, related-party exposures and private credit.

Related cases and compensation

ASIC sued the former directors of Keystone Asset Management, which ran the Shield Master Fund, in June; Shield took in more than A$530 million from about 5,800 investors. ASIC says it has sued every superannuation trustee that offered either fund, including Diversa Trustees, through which about A$300 million reached First Guardian, and Equity Trustees is defending its case. Macquarie has paid A$321 million to Shield investors, and Netwealth agreed to fully compensate First Guardian members at a cost of about A$100 million. ASIC said in May that more than A$420 million had been returned to investors.

Limits

This article summarizes a single trade-press report. The allegations are unproven and no court has made findings. It is general information, not legal or financial advice.

key_points: ASIC filed civil penalty proceedings in the Federal Court in October 2026 against David Anderson and Simon Selimaj, the former managing director and executive chairman of Falcon Capital, the First Guardian fund's responsible entity; the claims are allegations and have not been tested.

ASIC alleges that between August 2019 and April 2025 more than 6,000 Australians invested over A$600 million, mostly from superannuation, with about A$270 million going into unregistered underlying funds Falcon controlled and at least A$57 million to entities controlled by the two men.

Liquidators have recovered A$8.02 million, or 1.56%, of investments the directors valued at about A$512.8 million, with about A$344.5 million of mostly offshore property and early-stage technology investments returning nothing so far.

The Compensation Scheme of Last Resort raised its FY2027 estimate to A$198.1 million, including A$30.2 million for Shield and First Guardian claims, and Treasury's draft plan would charge managed investment scheme responsible entities A$40 million.

The public record does not show whether Falcon or its directors held directors and officers or professional indemnity cover; such policies typically exclude proven dishonesty and civil penalties are generally treated as uninsurable.
why_it_matters: Thousands of people's retirement savings were invested through a fund that has now collapsed, and the cost of compensating them is being spread across the financial industry through a levy. The case also tests how far liability insurance can respond when allegations involve conflicts and weak due diligence.
